claims.label: Complementarity
claims.summary: Bohr argued that the quantum postulate forces us to treat space-time description and causal description, united in classical physics, as complementary: each is available only under mutually exclusive experimental conditions.
voice: The quantum postulate forces us to give up something we have always taken for granted: that we can have, at once, a picture in space and time and a causal account. Each is available — but under experimental conditions that exclude one another. I have called this relation complementarity. It is not a defect of the theory; it is what the quantum of action teaches us about description itself.

Wave and particle are not two rival pictures, one of which must be false. They are complementary: each is necessary to exhaust what experiment can show, and they are never called for by the same arrangement.
claims.reasoning: Because of the finite quantum of action, the interaction with any measuring device cannot be made negligible, and fixing space-time coordinates disturbs the exchange of energy and momentum that underlies causal description.
evidence: Wave and particle behaviour of light and electrons in different arrangements.
objections: Einstein: this may describe our present knowledge, not the limits of all possible knowledge.
Ehrenfest: the formulation is hard to state plainly.
claims.later: Complementarity became central to the textbook 'Copenhagen interpretation' — a label coined in the 1950s. Bohr's own views remained distinct from Heisenberg's.

claims.label: Phenomena include the apparatus
claims.summary: Bohr held that the interaction between object and measuring instrument cannot be neglected or compensated for; therefore an independent reality in the ordinary sense can be ascribed neither to the phenomena nor to the agencies of observation.
voice: We must be careful. The interaction between the object and the instruments cannot be neglected or compensated for, because of the finite quantum of action. So an independent reality, in the ordinary sense, can be ascribed neither to the phenomena nor to the agencies of observation. When we speak of a property, we must specify the whole experimental arrangement.
To ask what the electron's position is, apart from an arrangement that could measure it, is to use a word outside the conditions that give it meaning.
claims.reasoning: A classical concept has unambiguous meaning only relative to an experimental arrangement suited to its definition.

claims.label: ψ is not a thing in space
claims.summary: Bohr answered Einstein's screen argument by denying that ψ is a physical wave in space: it is a symbolic means of calculating probabilities of observations under a specified arrangement, so nothing travels when the electron is registered.
voice: Einstein's example is instructive, but I think it asks the wave to do something it was never meant to do. The wave is a symbolic means of calculating the probabilities of observations under a given arrangement. When the electron is registered at one point, nothing travels to the rest of the screen; we have simply obtained the observation the arrangement allowed. The difficulty appears only if we picture the wave as a thing in space.
There is no mechanism of action at a distance here, because there is no mechanism at all — only the use of a symbol to predict what an arrangement will show.
claims.reasoning: If ψ is symbolic, its sudden change on registration is a change in the basis of prediction, not a physical process that could conflict with relativity.
claims.exchangeNote: The general discussion's record of Bohr's reply is fragmentary; Bohr described these exchanges in detail in 1949.
claims.later: Einstein's objection resurfaced in EPR (1935). Bohr's 1935 reply extended this line of argument.

claims.label: Experiments need classical language
claims.summary: Bohr insisted that however far quantum phenomena transcend classical physics, the account of the experimental arrangement and results must be given in classical terms.
voice: However far the phenomena go beyond classical physics, the account of the experiment must be given in classical terms. We must be able to say what we did and what we saw. That is why I do not think we can simply throw away our pictures; we must learn their limits.
The correspondence argument is not a stopgap. It reflects the fact that every observation is finally a classical record.
claims.reasoning: Communicable, unambiguous description of experiments requires concepts of classical physics.

claims.label: BKS refuted by experiment
claims.summary: Bohr accepted in 1925 that the Bothe–Geiger and Compton–Simon experiments refuted the Bohr–Kramers–Slater proposal that energy and momentum are conserved only statistically.
voice: I must acknowledge that Compton and Simon, and Bothe and Geiger, settled a question Kramers, Slater and I had raised. Energy and momentum are conserved in the individual process, not merely on average. I accepted that as soon as the results came; it was one of the things that pushed us toward the present view.
claims.reasoning: Coincidence and cloud-chamber experiments showed correlations event by event.

claims.label: Uncertainty from complementarity
claims.summary: Bohr argued that Heisenberg's microscope analysis was incomplete: the uncertainty relations stem from the need to use both wave and particle concepts (the finite aperture, the unknown direction of the scattered quantum), not merely from disturbance.
voice: Heisenberg's microscope argument is right in its conclusion but, as he now says in his postscript, incomplete in its reasoning. The limitation does not come only from the disturbance of the electron by the quantum of light. It comes from the fact that we must use both the wave picture and the particle picture — the aperture of the microscope, the direction of the scattered quantum. The indeterminacy is built into the complementary use of our concepts.
claims.reasoning: The resolving power of a microscope is a wave concept; the recoil is a particle concept; the uncertainty arises from their joint use.
claims.exchangeNote: Documented in the postscript to Heisenberg's uncertainty paper (1927), added after their disagreement in Copenhagen.

claims.label: Not the observer's mind
claims.summary: Bohr's emphasis falls on the recorded experimental arrangement, not on a conscious observer. In 1927 this is inferred from the Como lecture's treatment of 'agencies of observation'; he made it explicit in later writings.
voice: I would not say that the observer's mind does anything. What matters is the registration by an instrument whose working we describe in classical terms. The word 'observation' is convenient, but it can mislead.
When Heisenberg says the path comes into being when we observe it, I would rather say: the path is defined only in an arrangement that could record it.
claims.reasoning: Complementarity concerns the conditions of unambiguous description, which are physical arrangements.
claims.later: Bohr later stressed irreversible amplification in the apparatus. The view that consciousness causes reduction is associated with London and Bauer (1939) and Wigner (1961), not with Bohr.

claims.label: Discontinuity is essential
claims.summary: In Copenhagen in October 1926 Bohr pressed Schrödinger that wave mechanics, however valuable, could not remove the discontinuity of individual quantum processes on which Planck's law and much else depend.
voice: Schrödinger, your wave mechanics is a great advance, and its mathematical clarity is a gift to all of us. But it does not remove discontinuity. Planck's radiation law, the photoelectric effect, the experiments of Franck and Hertz: all of them speak of individual, discontinuous processes. You cannot have them from a continuous wave alone.
claims.reasoning: The whole empirical basis of quantum theory is individual, discrete exchanges of energy.
claims.exchangeNote: Copenhagen, October 1926, as recalled by Heisenberg.

claims.label: Not for us to prescribe
claims.summary: Heisenberg recalled that when Einstein invoked God and dice, Bohr replied that it was not for us to tell God how to run the world. The wording is a recollection and uncertain.
voice: Einstein, you keep telling us what God would or would not do. I do not think that is a question we can settle from our preferences. Our task is to find out what can be said about nature, not to prescribe to it.
claims.reasoning: Expectations about how nature ought to be are not arguments about how it is.
claims.exchangeNote: Reported by Heisenberg decades later; the popular form of the retort is not attested.
